title: Abattoir Process Control and Compliance Monitoring

lessons.title: Process control in practice
lessons.html:
Controlling the process, not just the product

Process control means keeping each step of the slaughter process within its set limits so that the product is right first time. In this work experience module you monitor and control processes across the abattoir under the guidance of a mentor, usually the foreman or production manager.

Control points to monitor

Control pointWhat is controlledHow it is checked
Ante-mortem and lairageWelfare, cleanliness, rest and waterObservation, lairage checklist
StunningEffective stun, stun-to-stick timeObservation of stun signs; sample timing
SterilisersWater temperatureThermometer readings recorded at set times
Dressing and eviscerationNo visible contaminationHourly sample of carcasses at a fixed point
Carcass washWater quality and pressureObservation; water test results
ChillingRoom and deep muscle temperatureData logger and probe readings
DispatchProduct temperature, marks, vehicle hygieneDispatch checklist
Condemned materialMarking, storage, disposalObservation and disposal records

Limits

Each control point has a limit set in the abattoir's hygiene management system or HACCP plan, for example the minimum steriliser temperature or the maximum carcass temperature at dispatch. Learn the limits for your abattoir and keep a copy in your notebook. Do not rely on memory or on what someone tells you on the floor.

Frequency

Monitoring must happen often enough to catch a problem before much product is affected. If a steriliser is checked only once a shift and fails early, hundreds of carcasses could be affected. Follow the frequency in the plan and increase it when a process is unstable.

lessons.title: Compliance monitoring and verification
lessons.html:
Monitoring versus verification

  • Monitoring is the routine checking done during production, such as recording steriliser temperatures every hour.
  • Verification checks that monitoring is being done properly and that the system works, for example reviewing the records at the end of the day, calibrating thermometers, observing the person doing the checks, and reviewing laboratory swab results.

As a foreman you will both monitor and verify. Verification is what auditors from the provincial veterinary services and customers look at closely.

Daily verification routine

  1. Review all monitoring records from the previous shift: complete, signed, values within limits.
  2. Where a value was out of limit, check that corrective action was recorded.
  3. Check that thermometers and scales are within calibration dates.
  4. Do a short walk-through observation of key control points.
  5. Sign the verification section of the records.

Weekly and monthly checks

  • Review trends in contamination findings, condemnations, temperatures and swab results.
  • Do an internal audit of one area using the hygiene audit checklist.
  • Check pest control reports and water test results.
  • Check training records against the skills matrix.
  • Follow up open corrective actions.

Internal audits

An internal audit is a planned, documented check of an area against requirements. Use a checklist, observe, ask workers to explain procedures, review records and note findings with evidence. Share findings with the supervisor of the area and agree on corrective actions and dates. Internal audits find problems before the external auditor does.

lessons.title: Building evidence and improving the system
lessons.html:
Your evidence

During this work experience, collect evidence that you can control processes and monitor compliance:

  • Monitoring records that you completed and signed.
  • Verification reviews you carried out, with notes on findings.
  • At least one internal audit report you prepared, with corrective actions followed up.
  • Trend charts you prepared and the actions they led to.
  • Logbook entries describing out-of-limit events and how you handled them.
  • Mentor observation reports.

Example logbook entry

Tuesday: verification of evisceration steriliser records found two hourly readings missing between 10:00 and 12:00. Spoke to supervisor; worker had been moved and no one took over the checks. Corrective action: checks assigned by station, not by person; added to start-of-shift allocation. Followed up Thursday: all readings complete.

Improving the system

Process control is not static. When you find repeated problems, ask whether the system itself needs to change:

  • Is the monitoring frequency enough?
  • Are the limits clear and correctly displayed at the station?
  • Are forms easy to use, or do they invite mistakes?
  • Do workers understand why the checks matter?
  • Would an automatic logger or alarm work better than manual checks?

Propose changes to your mentor and the quality manager with evidence. Changes to the HACCP plan or hygiene management system must follow the abattoir's document control procedure.

Key points

  • Process control keeps each step within set limits so product is right first time.
  • Know the limits and monitoring frequency for each control point.
  • Monitoring is routine checking; verification confirms that monitoring and the system work.
  • Use internal audits to find problems before external auditors do.
  • Collect specific, signed evidence and propose system improvements based on data.
